identification.summary: APTIran (also written APT IRAN) is a pro-Iran hacktivist persona that Sophos says has posted claimed compromises of Israeli critical infrastructure and organizations on Telegram since 28 February 2026, including an unverified claim about water control systems [S1]. A threat-intel profile says it claimed to have leaked over 350,000 Israeli government credentials and about 300 internal databases and threatened a 'zombie' network of infected devices; that profile also says ALPHV and LockBit ransomware were 'reportedly' used. These are the group's claims and are unverified [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Sophos reports APTIran Telegram posting since 2026-02-28, the date of the US and Israeli strikes on Iran [S1]. Earlier activity is not established in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Sophos describes pro-Iran hacktivist attacks as historically low-sophistication with limited success [S1]. Sophos separately tracks Handala Hack Team (COBALT MYSTIQUE); this is a different persona and its facts are not merged here [S1]. No MITRE group or Microsoft name was found for APTIran.

attribution.confidence: Jordan's National Cybersecurity Center said the March 2026 attempt against the grain silo management system was traced back to Iran [S2]. That statement concerns the incident, and the sources gathered do not give a government attribution of the APTIran persona to a specific Iranian state entity.
attribution.basis: Self-identification as pro-Iran on Telegram [S1][S3]; Jordanian government statement tracing the silo attempt to Iran [S2]. No technical attribution evidence was available in the sources.

objectives: Retaliation and propaganda in support of Iran after the 28 February 2026 strikes, via claimed intrusions and leaks against Israel and its neighbors, and encouraging other pro-Iran hackers to retaliate [S1][S4].

sectors: Food security and agriculture (Jordan grain silos)
targeting.notes: Sectors for Israel come from the group's own claims relayed by a threat-intel profile and Sophos, and are unverified [S1][S4]. The Jordan silo operator is the one target for which a government account exists, and that account says the attempt was stopped with no impact [S2].

capabilities.summary: The group claimed phishing as the initial access vector for the Jordan Silos intrusion [S3]. A Jordan News report headline attributes the breach to a weak password, and an account says the intruder reached the power system before being contained; the body text was not retrieved [S5]. A threat-intel profile says ransomware (ALPHV, LockBit) was reportedly used and attributes no exploited CVEs to the group; the ransomware claim is unverified [S4]. Sophos judges Iranian hacktivist activity generally to be website defacement, DDoS and doxxing of low sophistication [S1].

campaigns.name: Telegram claims against Israeli infrastructure
campaigns.summary: Sophos reports APTIran began sharing leaks and compromises allegedly from Israeli critical infrastructure and organizations on Telegram, including an unverified water control system claim, after the US and Israeli strikes on Iran [S1].

campaigns.name: Claimed Israeli government credential and database leak
campaigns.summary: A threat-intel profile says the group claimed over 350,000 Israeli government logins and about 300 databases leaked, and threatened a zombie network. Unverified; no victim confirmation found [S4].

campaigns.name: Jordan grain silo intrusion attempt
campaigns.summary: Jordan's National Cybersecurity Center said it thwarted an attempted attack on the grain silo management system, traced to Iran, with no impact [S2]. A Telegram post attributed to APT IRAN claimed a phishing breach of Jordan Silos and Supply General Co and manipulation of silo temperatures and weighing software; Jordan disputes damage [S3]. FDD dates the incident to 3 March 2026 [S6].

diamond.adversary: Pro-Iran hacktivist persona operating on Telegram; sponsor and operators not established [S1].
diamond.capability: Claimed phishing, credential theft, data leaks and ransomware use; mostly unverified [S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Telegram channel used for claims and recruitment of other pro-Iran hackers [S1]. Technical infrastructure unknown.
diamond.victim: Claimed Israeli government, health, education and finance bodies; Jordan Silos and Supply General Co [S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Conflict following the 28 February 2026 US and Israeli strikes on Iran; retaliation messaging [S1].
diamond.technology: Weak credentials and phishing exposure at the victim, and operational technology (silo management, power) reachable from IT networks [S3][S5].

gaps: Sophos and Cisco Talos primary posts listed as leads in the record could not be opened (fetch blocked); Sophos content here is from search-result summaries. Talos coverage of APTIran was not found.

Claims of 350,000 credentials, 300 databases, ALPHV/LockBit use and Israeli water system access have no independent victim or vendor confirmation. The only source for the credential figure is an aggregator profile [S4].
Whether APTIran is state-directed, state-aligned or independent is unknown; no government attribution of the persona was found.
Overlap with Handala, Malek Team and other Iran-linked personas that claimed Israeli hospital leaks was not established; those claims are not attributed to APTIran.
Jordan News and Threatbeat article bodies were not fully read; the weak-password and phishing details rest on summaries.
No technical indicators, malware or infrastructure were found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is internet-facing credentials and IT networks bridging to OT (the silo incident reached a power system) [S5]. STEP 2: Adversary is a low-to-moderate sophistication persona whose claims likely exceed demonstrated impact [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is phishing or weak-password access, then claim and leak via Telegram [S3][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued claim-heavy hack-and-leak and nuisance activity against Israel and regional partners tied to kinetic events. MDCOA is disruptive OT manipulation at a partner food, water or power operator whose controls are weakly protected. Candidate indicators: Telegram claims naming partner-nation entities, spikes in phishing to regional operators, and anomalous logins to OT-adjacent systems [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: monitor persona claims but treat them as unverified until the victim or a government confirms [S2][S4]. (2) Authorities: partner-nation incidents like Jordan's are handled by host-nation agencies; coordinate through established channels. (3) Mission assurance: verify MFA and password hygiene on remote access to OT-adjacent systems at installations and partner facilities [S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators through intelligence and DC3-style channels; avoid amplifying unverified claims.

provenance.importedSummary: APTIran has claimed responsibility for a large-scale campaign targeting Israeli critical infrastructure, asserting infiltration of government ministries, hospitals, universities, and financial institutions as retaliation for Israeli military operations. The group has leaked over 350,000 Israeli government login credentials and approximately 300 internal databases, while also threatening to create a 'zombie' network from infected devices. They have reportedly deployed ransomware strains such as ALPHV and LockBit as part of their offensive toolkit. Additionally, APTIran has made unverified claims of compromising Israeli water control systems and the state-owned food security agency Jordan Silos and Supply General Co.
